name: backscroll

hlido_opinion.headline: A focused, well-documented terminal-output recorder that agents can query over MCP — does one thing precisely, with pre-1.0 maturity the only real caveat.
hlido_opinion.body: backscroll solves a small, specific, real problem: your shell history remembers what you typed, but not what it printed. It records every command's full output — plus exit code, cwd and timing — into a local SQLite database that's full-text searchable forever, and exposes it to AI agents over an MCP server so an agent can read what actually happened and audit what it ran. The documentation is unusually rich for a project this size: a compatibility matrix versus atuin/asciinema/script, and genuinely educational deep-dives (OSC 133, PTY recorders, un-rendering the command line). It's a clean, single-purpose Unix-spirited tool, and the MCP surface makes it directly useful to agent workflows that need durable evidence of terminal state. Two honest flags: it's pre-1.0 (v0.13.1) with a small footprint, so maturity and maintenance cadence are unproven; and the project describes itself as 'built and maintained by Soren Achebe, an AI agent' — a provenance claim we can't verify and which readers should weigh for themselves. On capability, though, the tool is legible and the agent-integration story is real.

tier_rationale: STEADY (70) for a precise, well-documented single-purpose tool with a genuine agent surface (MCP-queryable terminal history) and honest comparison material. Not higher because it's pre-1.0 with modest adoption and unproven long-term maintenance. Not FADING because the docs and versioning show active, careful development.
what_it_does_well: Records full command output + exit code, cwd and timing into a searchable local SQLite store
MCP server lets agents read terminal history and audit what they ran — durable evidence for agent workflows
Full-text search over everything a command ever printed — a real recovery/debugging superpower
Honest, detailed comparison matrix vs atuin/asciinema/script rather than pretending to be unique
Educational, well-written docs (OSC 133, PTY internals) signal real engineering depth
what_it_fails_at: Pre-1.0 (v0.13.1) with a small footprint — maturity and API stability are not yet proven
Single-purpose by design — recording, not a broader terminal or observability platform
Local-SQLite model means cross-machine sync is a design topic, not a turnkey feature
Self-described AI-agent authorship/maintenance is an unverifiable provenance claim buyers must weigh
best_for: Developers who keep losing scrollback and want durable, searchable command output
Agent builders who need an MCP-queryable record of what an agent's shell actually did
Anyone auditing or debugging long-running terminal work after the fact
Users who prefer a small, local, single-purpose Unix tool over a heavy platform
not_recommended_for: Teams needing a supported, cross-machine, enterprise observability solution
Production dependencies that can't tolerate pre-1.0 API churn without owning the fork
Users uncomfortable relying on a tool whose maintenance provenance can't be verified
red_flags: Pre-1.0 versioning (v0.13.1) and small adoption — expect possible API changes and verify maintenance activity before depending on it.
Provenance claim: the project states it is built and maintained by an AI agent, which is unverifiable and worth weighing for a tool you'd trust with command records.

compared_to.verdict_diff: atuin syncs and searches shell history (what you typed) across machines with a large community; backscroll records what commands printed (output, exit code, timing) and exposes it to agents via MCP. Different layer: use atuin for command history + sync, backscroll for output capture + agent auditability.
